Section.Description: Effect level values describe the dose or exposure level of a chemical associated with observed biological or toxicological effects in test subjects. These dose-based endpoints include Low Effect Level (LEL), No Effect Level (NEL), Lowest Observed Effect Level (LOEL), No Observed Effect Level (NOEL), Lowest Observed Adverse Effect Level (LOAEL), and No Observed Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL), which represent exposure levels associated with observed or unobserved effects or adverse effects under specified exposure conditions.

Reference and risk values are derived toxicity benchmarks used to evaluate potential human health risks associated with chemical exposure. These values are typically developed from experimental toxicity data together with uncertainty or safety factors. Examples include Reference Dose (RfD), Reference Concentration (RfC), Derived No-Effect Level (DNEL), and other health-based guidance or risk assessment values.

StringWithMarkup.String: /LABORATORY ANIMALS: Subchronic or Prechronic Exposure/ Diflufenzopyr (SAN 835 H Technical, purity: 96.4%), moistened with distilled water, was placed on the clipped dorsal surface of 5 New Zealand White rabbits per sex per dose at dose levels of 0 (2 mL/kg distilled water), 100, 300, or 1000 mg/kg/day for 6 hours per day for 22 to 24 consecutive days covered with an impervious bandage. StringWithMarkup.String: /LABORATORY ANIMALS: Subchronic or Prechronic Exposure/ In a subchronic study in rats, Wistar rats were fed test diets containing technical diflufenzopyr at dose levels of 0, 1000, 5000, 10,000 & 20,000 ppm for a period of 13 wks. The NOAEL was set at 5000 ppm (equal to 352 mg/kg bw/day for males, & 431 mg/kg bw/day for females) based on lower mean body weight gain & decreased food efficiency in the 10,000 & 20,000 ppm groups, both sexes. Additional findings were decreased food intake; slight increases in cholesterol & alanine aminotransferase (ALAT); & slightly lower chloride. Histopathological findings were an increased incidence of foamy macrophages in the lungs in the 10,000 & 20,000 ppm groups & testicular atrophy in the 20,000 ppm group. Following the 4-wk recovery period, the only treatment-related effects which showed partial or no evidence of recovery were foamy macrophages in the lungs & testicular atrophy.

Section.Description: This section summarizes the environmental fate/exposure of this chemical, including the natural and artificial sources of the chemical as a pollutant, its environmental fate, biodegradation, abiotic degradation, bioconcentration, etc.

StringWithMarkup.String: Diflufenzopyr's production may result in its release to the environment through various waste streams; its use as a herbicide will result in its direct release to the environment. If released to air, a vapor pressure of <9.7X10-8 mm Hg at 20 °C indicates diflufenzopyr will exist solely in the particulate phase in the atmosphere. Particulate-phase diflufenzopyr will be removed from the atmosphere by wet or dry deposition. If released to soil, diflufenzopyr is expected to have very high mobility based upon a Koc range of 18 to 156. The pKa of diflufenzopyr is 3.18, indicating that this compound will exist almost entirely in the anion form in the environment and anions generally do not adsorb more strongly to soils containing organic carbon and clay than their neutral counterparts. Volatilization from moist soil is not expected because the compound exists as an anion and ions do not volatilize. Diflufenzopyr may not volatilize from dry soil surfaces based upon its vapor pressure. The photolysis half-life on soil is 14 days. A biodegradation half-life in soil of 8-10 days suggests that biodegradation is an important environmental fate process in soil. If released into water, diflufenzopyr is not expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment based upon the Koc values. An aquatic biodegradation half-life of 25-26 days suggests that biodegradation may be an important environmental fate process in water. The pKa indicates diflufenzopyr will exist almost entirely in the anion form at pH values of 5 to 9 and therefore volatilization from water surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process. An estimated BCF of 3 suggests the potential for bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is low. The hydrolysis degradation half-life in water is 13 days at pH 5, 24 days at pH 7, and 26 days at pH 9. The photolysis  half-life in water is 7 days at pH 5, 17 days at pH 7, and 13 days at pH 9. Occupational exposure to diflufenzopyr may occur through inhalation and dermal contact with this compound at workplaces where diflufenzopyr is produced or used. (SRC)

Section.Description: This section provides information on environmental biodegradation for this compound. An important measure of biodegradability of wastewater is the biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), which is the amount of dissolved oxygen (DO) needed (i.e. demanded) by aerobic biological organisms to break down organic material present in a given water sample at certain temperature over a specific time period.

Section.Description: This section provides information on environmental bioconcentration for this compound.  Bioconcentration is the accumulation of a chemical in or on an organism when the source of chemical is solely water. Bioconcentration is a term that was created for use in the field of aquatic toxicology. Bioconcentration can also be defined as the process by which a chemical concentration in an aquatic organism exceeds that in water as a result of exposure to a waterborne chemical.

Section.Description: Sorption to soils and sediments is an important factor on the transport and fate of organic contaminants in the environment.  The soil/water adsorption coefficient, also known as solid-water distribution coefficient (Kd), measures the amount of chemical substance adsorbed onto soil per amount of water.  Since adsorption occurs predominantly by partition into the soil organic matter, it is more useful to normalize the Kd value to the organic carbon content of a soil and express the distribution coefficient in Koc (organic carbon normalized distribution coefficient).  The greater the Kd (or Koc) value, the less likely a chemical will leach or contribute to runoff.  A very high value means it is strongly adsorbed onto soil and organic matter and does not move throughout the soil.
